title: Sri Chand the ascetic
hookLine: Nanak's elder son chose a celibate life; the Udasi order traces itself to him

cards: A family business, three generations in. The father built it. Everyone assumes the eldest will take the keys.
But the eldest's heart is somewhere else, and in the end the keys go to someone outside the family. Nobody is disowned. Families know this scene.
Guru Nanak's family knew it too. Today we follow his elder son, Sri Chand, who chose a life his father didn't choose. Today's word: Udasi.

teach.b: Sri Chand grew up while his father was out on the long road, and grew into a man drawn to stillness and renunciation.
Tradition remembers him as an ascetic: celibate, living apart from the household, devoted to meditation. He never married. And the Udasis, an order of renunciants, trace themselves to him.

teach.h: UDASI, AN ECHO OF THE JOURNEYS.
teach.b: Udasi is a word Sikhs already know from Nanak's own life, because the Guru's great journeys are called his udasis. So the son's order carries a name that echoes the father's travels.
Here's the tension, and the tellings don't hide it.

Guru Nanak's own way, as his hymns describe it, was the householder's way: earn honestly, share, remember God in the middle of family and work. He came home to Kartarpur, to the fields and the family.
And when it came time to choose who would carry the light after him, he didn't choose either son. He chose Lehna, and named him Angad. So what do the stories know?
They hold two things at once. Sikh teaching follows the householder path the Gurus walked.
And tradition still remembers Sri Chand with honor, as Baba Sri Chand, the Guru's son, a man of deep devotion who took a different road.
Tradition remembers later Gurus and Sri Chand meeting with respect, and Udasi teachers, it says, went on honoring Guru Nanak and singing his word.
That's how respect for a different choice looks in a family of faith: you don't pretend the roads are the same, and you don't stop calling each other family.

how: Sikhs follow the householder path the Gurus taught, and they remember Baba Sri Chand with respect as Guru Nanak's elder son and the figure the Udasi order traces itself to.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak's elder son. your father teaches the householder's life. you feel pulled toward stillness and renunciation. what do you do?
o: take over the household as expected.
follow the pull and live as an ascetic.
leave and never speak of your father again.
games.why: Sri Chand lived as a celibate ascetic, and the Udasi order traces itself to him. tradition still remembers him with honor.

practice: Bring to mind someone close who chose a road you didn't: a sibling who left the faith or entered it more deeply, a child who took a different city or a different kind of life.

Notice the old argument that rises, and don't try to settle it; just look at them, choosing, and find one thing in their choice you can honestly honor. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Udasi. The order of renunciants that traces itself to Baba Sri Chand, Guru Nanak's elder son, and a name that echoes the Guru's own journeys.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the name of the order that traces itself to Sri Chand, also used for Guru Nanak's journeys.

carryVoice: Your line: a different path. Not the same road, and still family. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.
